speechtext:
I am quite willing to discuss that too, and I will before I resume my seat. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), having made a close and careful investigation of his whole constituency, has just told us exactly what he found. I have similar information from other members. I know of individual cases of hardship; of course I do. A'ou would think, Mr. Chairman, when listening to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) this afternoon, that the only sympathy in the world for the unfortunate was manifested by the hon. gentleman when he left this country and spent his money to enjoy himself in France instead of staying at home. He has 'been reprimanding Canadians because they spend their money, whereas the economists of to-day are saying that rich men should spend and so put their money in circulation. Now the hon. member for Labelle says rich men are spending their money lavishly, and the people are getting the benefit of it, and they should not do so. That is one school of thought. The other is the school that says, "Save your money and put it in the bank; it will be safe there and no one will get any benefit from it." These two schools clearly indicate the differences of opinion that prevail with respect to the same matter.
I do not at this moment propose to answer hon. gentlemen opposite other than to say this. I never expected by remedial legislation to undo in a day the wrongs that had been done to this country in ten years. Neither did anybody expect it would be done, nor think it could be done. But this we do say, that within the time that has passed since accession to office no government has ever more fully Implemented its preelection promises *than the government now in power. I will not traverse the case made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). The minister who dealt with it as not in his place; he is ill. But we did say that where products were being dumped upon the Canadian market to the detriment of the Canadian producer, whether he be a nurseryman or a factory producer, such dumping was giving work to people outside of Canada that could be done by Canadians at home, and we proposed that Canadians should get that work through the instrumentality of government. Certainly we have no apology to offer for having said that.
Did you not at the same time say that prices would not be increased?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly. It is not a tariff item that the hon. gentleman is speaking of. There was no change in the tariff according to his own statement.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He has stated that there was no change in duty 'but that the value for duty was placed at 30 cents instead of 3 cents. That is what he has said. I am not in a position to determine whether or not the figures mentioned bear some adequate relation to the dumping of goods of a similar character upon this market because I have not the facts before me and did not know the matter was to be raised. Had I known it, I would have had the file brought to my attention.
This I desire to say, Mr. Chairman. Until the address has been adopted it would be wholly foreign to our parliamentary practice for the government to declare its policy. In the present instance the government is not acting as a government, it is simply the instrument to enable the public service to be carried on. Interim supply has been sought by succeeding governments, and it has never been made the occasion to raise questions of government policy, for the very obvious reason that the government cannot then make a declaration of policy, and should not do so. As I said a few moments ago, until the address is adopted it would be wholly foreign to our parliamentary institutions for the government to declare its policy. The best indication of what the government will do is to be found in what it has already done. Hon. gentlemen opposite nod their heads. They are opposed, I suppose, to the $20,000,000 having been voted for unemployment. Let this be borne in mind, that that $20,000,000 involves an expenditure during the next few months of over $75,000,000 on undertakings that, just as soon as conditions warrant, will be carried on. You cannot expect people to yield the wages that are being demanded without getting adequate results. This morning I was waited upon by a delegation urging that all the voluntary organizations that exist in this country to do useful service to mankind, churches, charitable and social organizations, should by statute be prevented from continuing their work. That is what I was asked to do by this delegation. Their slogan was "On the streets on the 15th of April." They came here this morning to urge upon the government non-contributory unemployment insurance. I told them they
Interim Supply

would never get it from any government that I had to do with; that is what I told them; I was perfectly frank about it. Whatever else this administration may lack, there is no lack of decision as to what it will do.
In due time and in the proper place I will answer the questions propounded by the leader of the opposition, not to-day but at the beginning of the short session. He may be desirous of giving us cooperation. Well, a little cooperation of patience in these days might do something; a little cooperation to get the speech from the throne adopted to enable us to settle down to business might be a useful effort. Look at what has happened this afternoon on a pro forma motion for one-sixth supply to enable the public services to be carried on. We have listened to what from the hon. gentleman from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)? He is one of the leading members of the Liberal party as now constituted, one of their front benchers, one of their most trusted lieutenants, one of the gentlemen in whom it reposes apparently the greatest trust, one who is accorded the heartiest applause and the loudest laughter by his colleagues beside him; he is given the cheer that always encourages further hope. This leading member of the Liberal party spent the afternoon reading upon Hansard words not spoken loud enough to be heard by the Hansard reporters, and then he handed them reams of material to be put on Hansard at the expense of the Canadian people, on the principle, I suppose, that money should be expended for the benefit of those who get out Hansard, for certainly it could serve no other purpose that anyone can suggest. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is a student of parliamentary institutions, and he knows perfectly well that this is not the time when the matter that he brought up can be dealt with. These are not ignorant men. If this pro forma motion for interim supply cannot ' be adopted this afternoon, the civil servants will be without their pay to-morrow, and they will know whom to blame for it. There is one party they cannot blame for it-the government.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has just made one statement which I think is entirely correct; he has said that according to the procedure of parliament until the address is adopted any other business should not be taken up, and that if other business is taken up it can only be by consent. May I point out to my right hon. friend that if there has been any occasion 	.
to vary that rule, the fault does not lie with an3'one but himself and the members of his administration. They did not call parliament until very late in the year, and surely the opposition or the country cannot be blamed for that circumstance. They brought parliament into session very late in the year, and naturally the whole public service was threatened with being inconvenienced because supply could not be voted in the regular way. Before the Easter recess my right hon. friend wished to get supply for the public service. We indicated our willingness to give him interim supply. Why did he not present the estimates to parliament before the Easter recess rather than now, on the loth of April? The beginning of the fiscal year is April 1, not April lo, and it was only yesterday or the day before that these estimates were laid on the table of the house. That is not the fault of the opposition; that is not due to any lack of cooperation or to any discourtesy on the part of the opposition. It is entirely the fault of my right hon. friend and his colleagues in not having the business of parliament ready when parliament was called and in being so late in the calling of parliament.
Now may I say this further word. When my right hon. friend requested the passing of supplementary estimates for the last fiscal year and later the passing of interim supply for the present year, it did require unanimous consent to have the right to suspend the regular procedure to allow the house to go into committee of supply to consider the estimates and this the opposition courteously granted. But when, through the courtesy of hon. members of the opposition and in fact of all hon. members of the house, the Prime Minister moved as a result of the consent given that the house go into committee of supply to consider the estimates, that motion carried with it the right, as it always has, whenever supply is considered, to any member to discuss any and every question in the nature of a grievance requiring redress and above all the right to discuss the most important question which is before the people of the country.
The debate on the address has run on for a considerable time, but during the course of the debate how much, may I ask, have we heard from the right hon. gentleman himself, or from a single minister of the crown with respect to the question of unemployment in this country? If the records are looked through from beginning to end it will be seen that we have had no statement from the ministry on that all-important question, a question so important as to necessitate,

Interim Supply
according to the view of the government, the calling of a special session of parliament last fall to deal with it. Under those circumstances it is not only the right but the duty of the opposition to demand from the government on every proper occasion what its policy is on this all-important question, and in doing so to-day we are only discharging the first duty of an opposition in seeking to get from the government some statement of policy.
I do not wish to go further into this question at the present time. I do think it would help throughout the country, in bringing about that better understanding of the government's position, if the Prime Minister would make at once a pronouncement to this house as to what the policy of the government is with respect to the unemployment situation which is so grave in Canada at the present time. I think the best way in which that statement could be made would be for him to give to the house and to the country quite frankly the meaning of his words when he said he would end unemployment. It is all right for my right hon. friend to say now that he did not mean he was going to end in one day the wrongs of ten years. I am not going to enter into any controversy about the wrongs of ten years or even as to how any conditions arose. That question can be debated by itself. My right hon. friend was dealing with a concrete condition of affairs in Canada during last summer, a condition of unemployment. True enough he did blame the then administration for that condition. The then administration was honest in saying that the condition was part of a world condition-
Oh, oh.
Were we not right in that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend said it did not exist.

No, we never
said anything of the kind. Over and over again I stated publicly that what we were suffering from in Canada was a world condition. I gave, as I saw them, a statement of the causes of unemployment and stressed very strongly the policy which I believed would more than anything else lead to an increase of trade. I stated that increase of trade would lead to an increase of work, and increase of work to a cessation of unemplojunent; that was the whole basis of the campaign, but my right hon. friend, dealing with concrete conditions, spoke of conditions of unemployment irrespective of their causes and said, "Return me to power and I will end unemployment." Now
I ask him again what he meant when he said, "I will end unemployment." It is not a good enough answer to give to the unemployed in this country to-day, or to the country, that he cannot do in one day what may have been occasioned by circumstances covering many years. He has been in power now for nearly nine months, and these estimates purport to deal with the expenditures for the next twelve months. Yet there is nothing here which indicates what is the policy of the administration. I do not intend to pursue this further at the moment, but I do intend to ask my right hon. friend when we take up the estimates again what he meant by the statement which I have just quoted, and I will expect him by that time to be prepared to give the country a satisfactory answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I
say that I think the attitude of the right hon. gentleman as expressed in his closing sentence is eminently fair and proper, and one which I shall endeavour to meet. I believe that to be the time and place to advance criticism and to meet criticism, and of course it is the right and duty of the opposition to criticize. I merely ventured to say I do not think that on any occasion heretofore when the government has been seeking pro forma supply in order to maintain the public service, any debate such as this has been indulged in. That was the point of my observations, and I can assure the right hon. gentleman that we shall endeavour to meet the suggestions he has made, I hope before we again have to consider any similar application such as this.

I should like to ask the
Prime Minister, in view of the fact that on the records of the house there are a large number of questions and notices of motion for the production of papers, whether we might have some guarantee that these papers will be produced before we take up the main estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can assure my hon, friend that while a number of these returns are voluminous, all those we believe should be properly brought before the house are in the course of preparation, and as soon as the address is adopted we believe we will be able to answer the questions without further delay.

Then there is another point to which I should like to refer, in connection with the matter brought up iby the hon. member for Sherbrooke. I refer to the matter of dumping. In discussing that point the right hon. Prime Minister said there was no increase in duty, but that these articles were being dumped on the Canadian market and
Interim Supply

therefore the dumping duty prevailed. If the matter is carefully looked into it will be found that at the very moment during the special session when parliament gave power to the Minister of National Revenue to apply the dump, so to speak, the price of the articles which would be affected in that way went up in Canada.
Not all of them.
But the hon. member must admit that the prices of some articles went up.
No.
The hon. gentleman is always ready to interrupt, but he does not know7 what he is talking about.
Yes I do.

Let the hon. gentleman
possess his soul in patience 'for a few moments. All he can do in the house is interrupt. Last session the hon. gentleman took up all his time in-I will not use that unparliamentary word "obstructing," but I mean that just the same. He took up the time of this house with very, very serious objections to certain ways of'carrying on the administration of some of the departments. Now he has taken up the time of the house interrupting speakers on this side. Let me say to him that we on this side of the house are not looking to him for any advice as to how we should proceed in matters of this kind.
You are not running the country.	[DOT]

No, we are not; nor is the government running this side of the house. We are running this side to suit ourselves. Perhaps the hon. gentleman who speaks about running the government is a little offended himself, a little sore because he was not taken in to run the government. There may be something in that if current rumours have any foundation at all. Now let me come back to the question of dumping. In this case the very moment the power was given directly to the minister to apply the dump the price of nursery stock in Canada went up, and on the increase of price the Department of National Revenue fixed the figure at which the dumping clause should apply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
How am I out of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Come to the item.
I am coming to the item. The Prime Minister spoke on this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Everyone has been out of order all afternoon.
[Mr. Veniot.)

Then I am not going to
be called down, surely. You are not going to make an example out of me when you allow everyone else to discuss it. I can stand on what I consider to be my rights, with all due respect to the chairman of committees. I was going to say that while the duty on nursery stock was not increased at the special session, nevertheless the fact that the minister had power to apply the dumping clause gave the producer in Canada the idea of increasing almost 80 per cent the price of nursery stock as it stood in August, 1930. That is how the injustice was done which, the hon. member for Sherbrooke spoke about.

I trust I
shall not be out of order inasmuch as what I am about to say affects the civil service. During the last two or three days I have been bringing up the question of the disposition of civil servants in the Department of the Interior who of necessity must either be placed in some other departments or be dismissed altogether. I wish also to correct an impression which some hon. gentlemen have, that nothing was done by the previous government to assist as far as humanly possible in transferring these civil servants. I am not going to take up the time of the house; I sympathize with the Prime Minister in his desire to get this interim supply through. But I do think that these people, some 150 or so, are entitled to know whether or not they are definitely out of the service, or whether the government is going to make some provision to place them in other departments when vacancies occur. I wish to make my position perfectly clear in this respect. I am not suggesting that the government paj' salaries while these men and women are not actively engaged in the civil service, but that they simply be kept on a reserve list and given preference when vacancies occur, over both promotions and entries to the service.

Does the hon. gentleman
suggest that, when a vacancy occurs in a department, all subordinate officials in that department who have been waiting fifteen or twenty years for advancement should be kept back while someone is taken from another department, such as the Department of the Interior, and put into that vacancy, over the heads of those who have been working in the department, who are familiar with its duties, and who are anxious for advancement therein?

Yes, I do
suggest that. If my hon. friend will look up the Civil Sendee Act he will see that

Interim Supply
frequently when examinations take place for promotions, they are not entirely confined to the department in question; other civil servants of similar standing may have an opportunity of competing for that position Now I quite appreciate the difficulties that arise in departments over matters of this kind, but I say that this is an exceptional situation and one which it is likely will never occur again in the history of the service, and I see no hardship that can occur to individuals who have to wait for perhaps a year for promotion, and more particularly to entries into the service.

I can call attention to cases
where they wait five and ten years.

I am quite
aware of that; but my hon. friend will agree that men who have fifteen or twenty years of service to their credit-and creditable service, may I say-are surely entitled to the same chance as an individual in a department. And indeed, in my own opinion, under the circumstances-
Mr .CAHAN:	The hon. gentleman suggested preference, not the same chance.
Yes, I do suggest a preference.
I just wish to understand the hon. gentleman.

That is my position; I wish to make it clear. And I wish also to make clear the fact that as far as possible junior members of the staff were transferred, foreseeing this difficulty. I wish only to be helpful and not critical; I have not offered one word of criticism. I know the difficulties, the serious difficulties, that arise when you undertake to transfer civil servants from one department to another. I quite appreciate that, but I do say that this is a very exceptional situation which is not likely to arise again in the course of many years.

speechtext: February of this year, the last month for which we have all the figures for the outside services. I say this to the hon. gentleman, there is no person charged with responsibility but can feel, shall I say sympathy?-or even more than that, alarm- at the duty which rests upon us. I put this to the committee: can we retain several hundred people without having anything for -them to do? That is the first question.
I trust my hon. friend is not assuming that I have asked him to do that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The second question is: what can we do to secure the transfer of these people to other branches of the public service? In my capacity as Minister of Finance I wrote to every one of my colleagues 
several weeks ago and stated: The last report which I have before me shows that you have on your pay list a certain number of temporary employees. I should like if you would be good enough to tell me why. In every instance they gave me a written memorandum dealing with the question whether or not it may be possible, looking to the future, to make provision for those who are engaged in, shall I say permanent places in the Department of the Interior. In the ultimate analysis the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy) has been able to provide for some members of the staff, but I say to this committee and to everyone affected, a very earnest desire has been evinced and will continue to be evinced to adjust the situation in as easy a manner as it is possible for those who are vitally affected, but we cannot and we dare not keep people in positions if there is nothing for them to do. I believe it is unthinkable that it should be suggested that we adopt t-hat action.
I know the former minister will not object to my mentioning the suggestion which he made the other evening. He said that in some instances it might be possible that parliament extend the period of service for the purpose of increasing the emolument which these civil servants .would receive under the Superannuation Act. I am informed that that would involve very serious consideration of the whole actuarial question, but I would inform my hon. friend that his suggestion has not been entirely discarded.
The hon. Minister of the Interior, whose sympathies are known to every person who is familiar with him in private life, has worried-I use that word deliberately-more over this matter than he has over any other matter of public service in his department. This involves the human factor and we do not have to be reminded of the nervous strain of those who are not quite sure of their positions, who are thinking of the morrow, who have obligations to meet and who desire to be in a position to meet them; that is in the minds of all of us.
False statements have been circulated with respect to this matter, and it is in no censorious sense that I draw to the attention of the committee just what pressure, political and otherwise, will do. This committee must realize the task we have had to meet, the difficulties we have had to overcome and the situation which confronts us, and I assure the committee that any suggestions offered will be gratefully received. There is a very earnest and anxious desire on the part of the administration to deal with those who are affected as they would expect to be dealt

Interim Supply
with by those who for the moment are charged with the responsibility of the administration of this country.

Mr. Chairman, there was one expression used by my right hon. friend which I think must have been an inadvertence on his part; either that, or it was made in ignorance of the exact facts. He referred to the temporary employees as being political favourites seeking jobs. My right hon. friend nods his head in assent. May I say to him that any such characterization is most unfair. My recollection is that when the late Liberal administration came into office we found many hundreds, I think I am safe in saying thousands of employees who were classified as temporary. Considerable of the time spent in straightening up civil service matters was consumed in the consideration of the position of these temporary employees, and my recollection is that throughout the time we were in office a very large number of those temporary employees were, to use the technical phrase, blanketed in; that is to say, they were made permanent employees.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By order in council.

By action of
the Civil Service Commission. What has actually taken place is that many employees who are styled as temporary have been longer in the public service than many of those who are classified as permanent. My impression is that all such were dealt with quite irrespective of their political complexion. They were blanketed into the permanent service because they had served so many years. I am sure that at the present time there are still a large number of civil servants designated as "temporary employees" who have been serving in their positions not for ten year's, but for fifteen or twenty years. I think it is entirely wrong to describe them as being political favourites who are seeking jobs. They are members of the public service of Canada who have been serving the country faithfully and because of a condition which I think might well be described as an injustice they have been carried along year after year as temporary employees when their services have in fact merited their being made permanent employees long ere this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

There is a case
of the librarian of the Department of the Secretary of State, Mr. Henry Roy, who is over seventy years of age, who has had forty years of service, who, in accordance with the Civil Service Act, is entitled to at least six months' leave of absence and who, I understand, has been dismissed from the service without a single day's leave notwithstanding the fact that the recommendation went from the department to the cabinet that he be given at least six months' leave of absence.

If my memory serves me
aright, no application was made by this librarian for leave of absence until after he had attained the age of seventy years or more, when he was bound to retire. Under the act he had to retire unless I could certify that he had some special qualifications which necessitated a continuance of his employment for another year. I do not wish to discuss the personnel of my department, but I could not give the certificate in that case. The librarian received every advantage that could be given to him under the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member for Rimouski has raised the question, might I point out that the section of the Civil Service Act states-and I am not responsible for it any more than the other members of the house are-that civil servants shall be retirable at the age of sixty-five, but at seventy they must retire unless their immediate head certifies that because of their peculiar fitness they should be continued in their positions. I did sign such a certificate the other day, but I put this to the committee: there is a gentleman seventy-three years of age and he had had a certificate for three years. It was signed again just as a matter of form, certifying that because of his peculiar fitness he should be continued in his position. What do hon. members think his position was? He was an elevator attendant. I give that illustration to show the difficulty the government experiences in matters of this kind. We did not raise the question, but when it is raised we must deal with it, and the only way you can escape it is to make a certificate of that character. The Secretary of State recalls the instance to which the hon. member for Rimouski refers. I think the hon. member for Rimouski will realize he would not ask the Secretary of State to make such a certificate.
Was the man of whom the Prime Minister spoke in his office? Mr. BENNETT: No.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: He is not flattered.

When he uses sarcasm about my humble self, I admit I feel very humble, but when I compare myself with any one of his ministers except the Minister of Justice who sits to his right, I feel reassured. I wish to continue to read this report.

speechtext: The resolution does not cover the railways; it simply covers the steamships, so my hon. friend is out of order.

There is nothing at all about the Canadian National Railways in it?
I he CHAIRMAN:	Only the Canadian
National steamships.

Resolutions reported.
I should like to put a question to the Prime Minister.
There is no motion before the house just now.

It is the reading of the resolution.
Mr. SPEAKER.: The reporting of the resolution is not debatable.

I wish to speak to a question of privilege. When the first resolution was introduced, I asked the Prime Minister whether it- had something to do with the Canadian National Railways, and he said that it had not but that he was going to bring in another one that would have something to do with them. The Chairman has just said that the second resolution included nothing in connection with the Canadian National Railways. I do not know whether the Prime Minister made a slip or not, and I would like to be posted on the matter.
